lab00-s000.title: Before You Start This Lab
lab00-s000.markdown:
**Estimated time:** 15 minutes
**Module goal:** Prepare an environment for the exercises and understand the costs incurred by this workload before you begin. ---

lab00-s001.title: Workshop Environment and Target Folder
lab00-s001.markdown:
Open the exercise workspace and folder specified by your instructor or Fabric administrator, and confirm that it is not a production environment. Before starting, also ask the administrator to confirm the capacity SKU, region, and available resources. The displayed capacity allocation alone does not indicate performance, headroom, or cost under concurrent use.

The folders, models, permissions, and billing conditions used for the exercises vary by workshop environment. Replace sample names in the text with the names in your actual environment, and do not record tenant-specific identifiers or credentials in the materials.

lab00-s002.title: What to Check in the Admin Portal
lab00-s002.markdown:
1. Open the specified exercise workspace and folder. Confirm with the instructor or administrator that this is the expected location and not a production environment.
2. Open **Workspace settings** → **Workspace type** and check Current workspace type, assigned capacity, SKU, Region, and Semantic model storage format. Do not copy names or IDs into workshop records; check only the values you need.

   ![Example of checking capacity assignment and SKU in Workspace type. Specific capacity information is obscured.](../assets/screenshots/lab00/capacity-assignment.png)

3. In the Fabric Admin portal, open **Tenant settings** and confirm the Planner, Stakeholder, and Oversubscription Warning settings and their scopes with the administrator. If a change is needed, limit its scope according to your organization's policy. Do not enable organization-wide settings without conditions.

   ![Example of reviewing the Planner upgrade setting and scope in Tenant settings. Specific current values are obscured.](../assets/screenshots/lab00/tenant-planner-setting.png)

   ![Example of reviewing the Stakeholder upgrade setting and scope in Tenant settings. Specific current values are obscured.](../assets/screenshots/lab00/tenant-stakeholder-setting.png)

   ![Example of reviewing the Oversubscription Warning setting in Tenant settings. Specific current values are obscured.](../assets/screenshots/lab00/tenant-oversubscription-setting.png)

4. In the Fabric Admin portal, open **Tenant settings** and check the status and scope of **Integration settings** → *Allow XMLA endpoints and Analyze in Excel with on-premises semantic models*. Then open **Admin portal** → **Capacity settings** → the target capacity → **Power BI workloads** and check **XMLA Endpoint**. This exercise requires Read Only or Read Write. Check workspace and model permissions separately.

   ![Example of checking XMLA Endpoint in capacity settings. Confirm with the administrator whether Read Only or Read Write is required in the target environment.](../assets/screenshots/lab00/capacity-xmla-endpoint.png)

5. In the workspace's **Manage access**, check the role of the person creating the items. The operational recommendation for this exercise is to assign the creator Member or Admin. The person connecting the model needs Read and Build on the semantic model; Read is sufficient just to view an already-connected model. Do not grant more permissions than necessary.
6. To test regional viewing, explicitly assign the applicable model role to a Viewer and verify the viewing scope with a separate user. Do not assume what happens when no role is assigned; follow the [RLS procedure in Module 08](08-sizing-and-governance.md#行レベルセキュリティの運用).

---

lab00-s003.title: The Scenario
lab00-s003.markdown:
Harborlight Provisions had FY25 revenue of approximately **US$25.9 million ($25.9M)**. The board initially requested an FY26 target of **US$28.5 million ($28.5M)**, then raised it to **US$30 million in revenue ($30M) and US$12.5 million in gross profit ($12.5M)**. The business, which grew 5% the previous year, is now aiming for growth of about 16%.

The current planning process uses an Excel workbook with 40 worksheets. Finance leads for three regions each manage their own sheets, and headquarters consolidates them. But when someone changes a formula, the regional sheets become inconsistent, so no one trusts the consolidated results. Last year's forecast reached the board 11 days after it was prepared. By then, it was already out of date.

All the data needed for planning is in a well-managed Power BI semantic model used for monthly reporting. The plan itself, however, is separate from that model.

The next eight modules will change this situation.

---

lab00-s004.title: What Is Fabric Planning?
lab00-s004.markdown:
Fabric Planning is a workload for enterprise performance management built into Microsoft Fabric as part of Fabric IQ. It lets you use the semantic model used for analytics to create budgets, forecasts, and scenarios, avoiding inconsistencies in number definitions between planning and actuals.

It has four components. This exercise uses the first three and also introduces the fourth.

| Component | Primary purpose | Related modules |
|---|---|---|
| **Planning sheets** | Create budgets, forecasts, and scenarios in an Excel-like grid based on a semantic model | Modules 01–05 |
| **Intelligence sheets** | Create report canvases, variance analysis charts, KPI cards, and financial matrices | Module 06 |
| **PowerTable** | Manage reference and master data, and create data apps with forms, approvals, and automation | Module 07 |
| **Infobridge** | Link data and planning, for example by automatically consolidating regional sheet plans at headquarters | Module 08 |

---

lab00-s005.title: Before You Start: How Billing Works
lab00-s005.markdown:
Fabric Planning is billed based on **active 30-day sessions**, not per-user licenses.

A session starts when a user opens, creates, or edits a Plan item. As stated in the official documentation, a session **lasts 30 days (730 hours) and cannot be ended early**.

> [!NOTE]
> **Note:** The [official billing documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/iq/plan/resources/billing-fabric-plan) says “30 days (730 hours)” and also uses 730 hours in its estimates. However, 30 calendar days is 720 hours. The calculations in this exercise use the official example's 730 hours. Check the actual session expiration and billing in the admin portal and billing information.

The role-based consumption below applies to the **Planning workload only**. Fabric SQL, OneLake, and Power BI XMLA operations consume capacity separately. This is why the latter part of this module allows for 30% headroom.

| Role | Typical users | Per session over 30 days |
|---|---|---|
| **Planner** | FP&A professionals, model creators, administrators | **847 CU hours** |
| **Stakeholder** | Business users, reviewers, approvers | **168 CU hours** |
| **Viewer** | Executives, report viewers | **37 CU hours** |

lab00-s006.title: CU Hours and CU Are Different
lab00-s006.parent: Before You Start: How Billing Works
lab00-s006.markdown:
This distinction is easy to mix up even after reading the documentation, so let's clarify it here.

Imagine a faucet that flows at **4 liters per minute**. That is 240 liters in an hour and 5,760 liters in a day. The faucet itself has not changed; only the measurement period has.

Capacity works the same way. **F4 is like a faucet with processing capacity of 4 CU.** The baseline is 4 CU, which can be expressed as follows depending on the measurement period.

| Measurement period | The same F4 expressed as available consumption |
|---|---|
| 1 second | 4 CU-seconds |
| 1 hour | 14,400 CU-seconds (4 × 3,600) |
| The official example's 730 hours | 2,920 CU hours (4 × 730) |

Every row represents the same “4 CU.” The Fabric Capacity Metrics app displays values per hour because it checks processing over short time intervals. In contrast, the Planning billing article explains the total for one session using a 730-hour calculation example. The capacity is the same; only the purpose of the measurement differs.

In other words, **CU is processing capacity, while CU hours are the amount consumed over a period of time**. A Planner does not require F847. Just as using a 1,000-watt heater for 10 hours does not require a 10,000-watt power supply, distributing 847 CU hours across the official example's 730 hours gives an average consumption of **a little over 1 CU**.

| Role | Per session over 30 days | Average consumption over the official example's 730 hours |
|---|---|---|
| **Planner** | 847 CU hours | **1.16 CU** |
| **Stakeholder** | 168 CU hours | **0.23 CU** |
| **Viewer** | 37 CU hours | **0.05 CU** |

#### Compare the same time period

Comparing what capacity can supply with what users consume over different periods leads to calculation errors. Align the periods first.

Compare one Planner's use of F4 over two periods:

| Comparison period | Amount F4 can supply | Planner consumption | Remaining |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Per hour** | 14,400 CU-seconds | 4,177 CU-seconds | **10,223 CU-seconds, about 71%** |
| **Per 730 hours in the official example** | 2,920 CU hours | 847 CU hours | **2,073 CU hours, about 71%** |

The result is the same either way. One Planner accounts for **about 29% of F4**.

Be careful not to compare across rows. Subtracting the Planner's 30-day consumption of 847 from one hour of supply, 14,400, gives the plausible-looking value 13,553. This makes the Planner's consumption look like about 6%, underestimating it by a factor of about five. Because the number itself does not look unreasonable, this error can go unnoticed even in a meeting.

To convert units, use **CU hours × 3,600 = CU-seconds** and **CU hours ÷ 730 = average consumption (CU)**.

lab00-s007.title: Billing Is Per Session, Not Per Month
lab00-s007.parent: Before You Start: How Billing Works
lab00-s007.markdown:
This distinction matters when you consider costs. A session does not start on the first day of each month; it lasts 30 days **from the time an action starts it**. There is no additional session charge for using it every day during this period. Repeating an action with the same role, tenant, and capacity does not start a second session. After the period ends, a new session starts **only when you take an action again**.

Annual consumption therefore depends on actual usage, not the number of people on staff.

| Usage pattern | Sessions per year | Annual Planner consumption (CU hours) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Continuous use (estimated as 12 sessions) | 12 | 10,164 |
| Update the forecast quarterly | 4 | 3,388 |
| Use only during the budgeting period (3 months) | 3 | 2,541 |
| Open once in March | 1 | 847 |

> [!NOTE]
> **Translation note:** The estimate of 12 sessions per year is from the original. Sessions are not calendar-month based, so the number of starts during continuous use and billing across fiscal years depend on the start date and renewal timing. Recalculate using the actual period when budgeting.

This is an important point when comparing with per-user EPM licenses. Occasional reviewers and approvers incur a session only when they participate. For example, a CFO who approves only twice a year is treated as having two Stakeholder sessions per year, rather than one annual license seat.

> [!NOTE]
> **Correction to the original:** The original uses Viewer for this example, but the [official role definitions](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/iq/plan/overview-roles) classify approval actions as Stakeholder. The Japanese edition corrects this to Stakeholder. Viewer applies to read-only access. If other actions result in a higher role, that role's billing applies.

There is an important tradeoff. A session cannot be ended early, so someone who touches a plan just once on the first day and someone who works on it every day for 30 days incur the same session consumption. Infrequent use during a session does not reduce consumption.

lab00-s008.title: Consider Capacity in Practice
lab00-s008.parent: Before You Start: How Billing Works
lab00-s008.markdown:
Capacity supplies CU continuously, so over a 730-hour period it can provide **CU × 730 CU hours**. One Planner session consumes 847 CU hours of that amount.

| SKU | Supply over the official example's 730 hours (CU hours) | 1 Planner | Team of 10 (1,704) | With 30% headroom (2,215) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **F2** | 1,460 | 58% | **117%, insufficient capacity** | **152%, insufficient capacity** |
| **F4** | 2,920 | 29% | 58% | 76% |
| **F8** | 5,840 | 15% | 29% | 38% |
| **F16** | 11,680 | 7% | 15% | 19% |
| **F32** | 23,360 | 4% | 7% | 9% |
| **F64** | 46,720 | 2% | 4% | 5% |

The 10-person team consists of one Planner, four Stakeholders, and five Viewers, as estimated in [Module 08](08-sizing-and-governance.md).

There are two important caveats. First, this view checks a **consumption budget**, not processing performance. It shows whether consumption fits within capacity over 30 days, but not whether throttling will occur at 9 a.m. on Monday. Also, **capacity is shared with all other Fabric workloads**. If a Warehouse or semantic model refresh is already running on F8, Planning consumption is added on top of it.

lab00-s009.title: Pausing Capacity Does Not Eliminate Session Costs
lab00-s009.parent: Before You Start: How Billing Works
lab00-s009.markdown:
If capacity is paused or deleted during a session, **the remaining CU consumption for each active session is added together and charged to Azure**. Pausing does not defer the cost; it accelerates billing. Even if you start a Planner session on Monday and stop the capacity on Tuesday, the remaining 28 days are billed.

Also keep the following points in mind:

- **Deleting the Plan item does not stop the session.** Active sessions continue for 30 days and are billed, whether or not the item still exists.
- **Running out of capacity does not stop the session.** The session continues to be recorded and billed periodically even when other workloads have consumed all available credits.

lab00-s010.title: Billing Roles Depend on What You Do
lab00-s010.parent: Before You Start: How Billing Works
lab00-s010.markdown:
Everyone starts as a Viewer. The system upgrades the role in response to your actions.

- Simply **opening and viewing** a sheet keeps you at **Viewer**.
- **Entering or changing plan values, approving, writing back, or creating or editing a PowerTable or Intelligence sheet** makes you a **Stakeholder**.
- **Creating a planning sheet or editing its design** makes you a **Planner**. Design includes changing structure, rules, and the writeback destination. A person who creates a new Plan item also becomes a Planner.

> [!NOTE]
> Before August 19, 2026, people who created PowerTable or Intelligence reports also became Planners. This is no longer the case. Older materials that say otherwise describe the previous behavior.

Keep these three points in mind:

1. **A role upgrade starts a new session.** The lower-role session ends and is prorated; billing then switches to the higher role. You cannot downgrade a role during an active session.
2. **For the same user and capacity, billing is at the highest role reached.** However, using two capacities results in two sessions.
3. **Automation jobs are billed separately.** Each successful PowerTable automation or planning integration instance consumes **2 CU** per run. Failed jobs are not billed.

Fabric SQL, OneLake, and XMLA operations consume capacity outside the Planning meter as well, so allow **about 30% headroom**.

lab00-s011.title: Administrator Controls
lab00-s011.parent: Before You Start: How Billing Works
lab00-s011.markdown:
Administrators can control when sessions start and roles are upgraded. The following three tenant settings control which users can upgrade their roles.

| Setting | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Users can upgrade to a Planner session** | Allow or prevent upgrades to Planner for the entire organization or specified security groups |
| **Users can upgrade to a Stakeholder session** | Similarly control upgrades to Stakeholder |
| **Show Oversubscription Warning** | Display a warning before starting or upgrading a session expected to oversubscribe capacity |

These three settings can be overridden for each capacity using **Delegated Tenant Settings**. Planner access includes Stakeholder access, so allowing Planner across the organization also allows Stakeholder across the organization. Users who are allowed neither role can still open a Plan item in Reading view.

**For this exercise:** Completing Module 01 makes you a Planner and starts a session that consumes 847 CU hours over 30 days. A trial capacity can be used at no charge. If you are using a shared production F SKU, calculate the required amount first. Microsoft's [capacity estimation tool](https://community.fabricplan.com/capacity-pricing/) may also help with this estimate.

After trying the actions associated with each role, revisit the capacity estimate in Module 08.

---

lab00-s012.title: Prerequisites Checklist
lab00-s012.markdown: Check the following items in order. If any of the first three are missing, the exercises may be blocked by errors whose cause is difficult to identify.

lab00-s013.title: 1. Capacity
lab00-s013.markdown:
- [ ] Confirm that you have a Microsoft Fabric capacity of **F2 or higher**, or an active [Fabric trial](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/fundamentals/fabric-trial).

Power BI Pro and Premium Per User are **not supported** for the XMLA and embedded-token scenarios used in this exercise. Power BI Premium P1–P5 can be used. Even on supported capacities, smaller SKUs may reach XMLA or memory limits.

lab00-s014.title: 2. Workspace Roles
lab00-s014.markdown:
- [ ] As an operational recommendation for this exercise, assign the necessary people the **Member** or **Admin** role in the workspace before the workshop.
- [ ] The person connecting the model to the Plan item must have both **Read and Build** permissions on the semantic model. Read is sufficient just to reference a model that is already connected.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Correction to the original and discrepancy between official sources:** The original and [Tutorial Part 0](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/iq/plan/planning-tutorial/planning/tutorial-0-introduction) say Contributor is insufficient, while the current [official FAQ](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/iq/plan/resources/frequently-asked-questions) says Contributor or higher can create a Plan. The Japanese edition does not assert that “Contributor is categorically unsupported”; it recommends Member or higher to help the exercise run smoothly. For production permission design, verify the connection and sharing methods in the workshop tenant in advance and grant only the permissions needed. See [Troubleshooting semantic model connections](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/iq/plan/planning-troubleshoot-semantic-model) for the model's Read / Build requirements.

lab00-s015.title: 3. Tenant Settings
lab00-s015.markdown:
An administrator enables the following in **Tenant settings** in the Fabric Admin portal.

- [ ] **Integration settings** → *Allow XMLA endpoints and Analyze in Excel with on-premises semantic models*
- [ ] The original lists **Developer settings** → *Embed content in apps*, but this is not listed as a required setting in the current [prerequisites](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/iq/plan/overview-prerequisites). The administrator should confirm in advance whether it is needed in an environment using the older procedure.
- [ ] **Developer settings** → *Service principals can call Fabric public APIs* (required only when authenticating with a service principal)

lab00-s016.title: 4. Capacity Settings
lab00-s016.markdown:
- [ ] Check the XMLA Endpoint setting with the administrator. Read Only or Read Write is required.
- [ ] Confirm that the capacity SKU, region, and administration policies support the features used in the exercise.

Even with XMLA Endpoint set to Read Write, this does not guarantee that the Plan can start, connect to the model, or support subsequent operations. Check workspace, model, and tenant permissions and settings separately.

lab00-s017.title: 5. Browser
lab00-s017.markdown:
- [ ] Use Microsoft Edge or Google Chrome. **Safari is not supported.**
- [ ] Confirm with the administrator that organizational browser policies, authentication, and network settings allow access to the exercise screens.

If a screen is blank or you cannot open the Plan, check that the supported browser is up to date, and review organizational policies and connection permissions with the administrator. Do not broadly weaken security settings such as cookies or TLS without first identifying the cause.

lab00-s018.title: 6. Sample Data
lab00-s018.markdown:
- [ ] Download **`Northwind_FMCG.pbix`** from Microsoft's sample repository, [fabric-samples/docs-samples/iq/plan](https://github.com/microsoft/fabric-samples/tree/main/docs-samples/iq/plan).

If you will also complete the optional PowerTable module, download `Northwind-FMCG-assets-powertable-tutorial.xlsx` from the same folder.

See [`data/README.md`](../data/README.md) for details about the model.

---

lab00-s019.title: “Can I Use It Without a Semantic Model?”
lab00-s019.markdown:
This is a common question about Planning, but the answer needs a little explanation. Let's clarify it before we begin.

First, Planning connects to a **semantic model**, not a report. A Power BI report is not required for the connection. Some organizations use a managed model through Excel or Analyze in Excel without creating formal reports. Planning connects through XMLA, so it does not matter whether a report exists.

What matters is the state of the model. Consider these three cases.

lab00-s020.title: There Is a Model, but No Report
lab00-s020.parent: “Can I Use It Without a Semantic Model?”
lab00-s020.markdown: That is fine. Connect the Plan item to the model to complete the modules in this exercise. Replace the first step of importing the sample with “select an existing model.”

lab00-s021.title: There Is Data in Fabric, but No Model
lab00-s021.parent: “Can I Use It Without a Semantic Model?”
lab00-s021.markdown: First create a semantic model on a Lakehouse or Warehouse. Direct Lake is also supported. However, there are settings to understand in advance. The original says that **Direct Lake and DirectQuery models require a gateway connection with fixed credentials and do not support single sign-on**. The current [procedure for creating a planning sheet](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/iq/plan/planning-how-to-get-started), however, describes direct connection with the signed-in user's ID rather than a shared cloud connection. Do not apply the original gateway requirement to every current configuration. Verify the connection using the combination of storage mode, data source, and authentication method for the model you plan to use.

lab00-s022.title: There Is No Data or Model
lab00-s022.parent: “Can I Use It Without a Semantic Model?”
lab00-s022.markdown:
Planning also offers ways to get started without a model.

| Starting point | Data and operations accepted |
|---|---|
| Create a Plan item | Import data from a semantic model **or Excel**, or create a planning sheet first and connect data later |
| PowerTable **New Table** | Create a blank table for manual entry using Excel, CSV, or just column headers |
| Intelligence sheets | Import Excel and CSV files |

These are also supported ways to use the product. The role documentation also mentions Plan items containing only PowerTable or only an Intelligence sheet.

**However, consider whether this approach fits your purpose before recommending it.** The tutorials, prerequisites, and permission descriptions are all centered on connecting to a semantic model. There are relatively few published procedures or examples for starting from Excel.

It is also important to check whether the approach addresses the problem you are trying to solve. If an organization without a semantic model simply uploads spreadsheets to Planning, it still lacks consistent number definitions and governance. Moving a workbook with 40 sheets into Fabric alone does not fundamentally improve the process.

The recommended sequence is to bring actuals into Fabric, establish a semantic model, and then create plans on that model. Planning's value is that plans and actuals can use common, managed definitions. Without that foundation, it remains a spreadsheet with an approval workflow.

Starting from files is appropriate for **reference or master data** that has no formal system of record, such as a list of cost centers, a staff list, or an asset register. [Module 07](07-powertable.md) covers exactly this use case. This is also why PowerTable accepts Excel while planning sheets are centered on models.

---

lab00-s023.title: Limitations to Know in Advance
lab00-s023.markdown:
Review these limitations now so that you can identify the cause if you encounter the same behavior later.

| Limitation | Impact |
|---|---|
| Microsoft Entra **B2B guest accounts** | The original and tutorial say these are unsupported, but current error-resolution material also includes a workaround using guest database permissions. Their use cannot be categorically ruled out; validate before the workshop. |
| **Private links** | Correction to the original: workspace-level private links are unsupported, but current limitations say tenant-level private links are supported. |
| Semantic models in **My workspace** | Cannot be used. |
| **Composite models** | Correction to the original: these are now supported. Whether a specific configuration works depends on storage mode, data source, authentication, and other factors. |
| Semantic model permissions | The person connecting the model needs **Read and Build**. Read is sufficient just to reference an already-connected model. |
| **Renaming a semantic model** | The connection breaks, and the Plan item stops working. |
| **Renaming a workspace** | The Plan item can no longer be opened. |
| One semantic model per Plan item | The connection **cannot be changed**. A new Plan item is required to use a different source. |



Also confirm the connection method and authentication requirements for the target model if you use Direct Lake / DirectQuery.

> [!NOTE]
> **Basis for differences from the original:** Composite models and private links are covered in the [current limitations](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/iq/plan/overview-limitations); connection permissions are covered in [troubleshooting model connections](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/iq/plan/planning-troubleshoot-semantic-model); and the example involving guest database permissions appears in [error codes and resolutions](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/iq/plan/resources/error-codes-and-resolutions). If using guests, an administrator must validate the setup, including the organization's external sharing policies.

Pay particular attention to the last point. Once Module 01 creates a Plan item and connects it to a model, that combination is fixed for as long as you use the item. Choose the connection carefully.

---

lab00-s024.title: What Is Created Automatically
lab00-s024.markdown:
In the original configuration, **a Fabric SQL database is automatically created in the workspace** to store Plan item metadata. You do not need to create it yourself in that configuration.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Discrepancy between official sources:** The [prerequisites](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/iq/plan/overview-prerequisites) and [procedure for creating a planning sheet](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/iq/plan/planning-how-to-get-started) describe automatic creation of a SQL database. The [official FAQ](https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/iq/plan/resources/frequently-asked-questions), however, says that new Plan items store app metadata in OneLake and that the database connection for collaboration is deprecated. Therefore, do not assume the presence or number of automatically created databases; check the actual workshop tenant. Do not delete anything without checking the storage location for existing Plans. The database count below describes the original SQL configuration.

This is separate from the **writeback destination** configured later. The writeback destination stores plan values so they can be referenced by other Fabric features. It is explicitly configured in Module 04.

lab00-s025.title: Fabric SQL Costs Are Separate from Role-Based Consumption
lab00-s025.markdown:
Each Fabric SQL database is billed for **compute and storage** independently of the Planning meter.

- **Compute** scales automatically. While the database is online, at least 2 GB of memory is billable. If there is no activity for 15 minutes, compute consumption becomes zero. The database remains online for 15 minutes after the last query, so even if you work for only 2 minutes, billing time is about 17 minutes.
- **Storage** continues to be billed **even when compute is stopped**. Charges include allocated storage and backup storage exceeding 100% of the provisioned database size.

Storage costs continue to accrue if you leave the exercise environment as it is. The 30-day session also continues, whether or not you open it again.

> [!WARNING]
> **Note about the original trial and SQL configuration:** The original says trial capacity is limited to three SQL databases. The number needed depends on the current metadata storage method, so do not apply the following count as-is to the workshop environment.
>
> Completing all modules creates the following four databases:
>
> | # | Database | Created in module |
> |---|---|---|
> | 1 | `Northwind_FMCG_YourName`: writeback destination | Module 01 |
> | 2 | Database for Plan item metadata: automatically created | Module 01 |
> | 3 | `fabric_plan_training` | Module 07 |
> | 4 | Database for the second Plan item's metadata: automatically created | Module 07 |
>
> In this configuration, the list shows only two databases required for Modules 00–06 and 08, which does not match the original claim that the limit is “exactly reached.” **Adding Module 07 brings the total to four, so it cannot be created in a trial subject to the three-database limit.** In that case, the error `GEN_DB_010` (*"SQL database capacity limit reached, so a new plan item can't be created."*) appears. It means the SQL database capacity limit has been reached and a new Plan item cannot be created.
>


> Have the administrator confirm the required artifacts and storage locations, and use a separate validated environment or paid capacity. Also check the trial size at **Capacity settings** → **Trial**. A trial is provisioned as **F4 or F64**, and its size may be changeable depending on conditions.

---

lab00-s026.title: Knowledge Check
lab00-s026.markdown:
Before continuing, try answering the following questions.

1. Why does this exercise recommend Member or higher in advance? What discrepancy is there among official sources regarding Contributor?
2. What actions make you a Planner, and how many CU hours does the session consume?
3. If the work is finished in one day, can you end the Planning session early?
4. What happens if you rename the workspace containing the Plan item?
5. One Planner session consumes 847 CU hours. What proportion of F4 is this?
6. Can an organization without any Power BI reports use Planning?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. To help the original exercise procedures, including connection and collaboration, run smoothly. The tutorial requires Member/Admin, while the current FAQ says Contributor or higher can create a Plan. Do not categorically rule out Contributor; validate the operations and permissions needed in the workshop environment.
2. Creating a Plan item, creating a planning sheet, or changing the design of a planning sheet. This starts a 30-day Planner session that consumes 847 CU hours.
3. No. Once started, it lasts 730 hours and cannot be ended manually.
4. The Plan item can no longer be opened.
5. An average of 1.16 CU, or about 29% of F4. Divide 847 by the session's 730 hours. Comparing 847 with one hour of supply underestimates the consumption proportion by about a factor of five.
6. Yes. Planning connects to a semantic model, not to a report. The important question is whether a managed semantic model exists.

</details>
